Plato ( / ˈ p l eɪ t oʊ / PLAY -toe ; Ancient Greek : Πλάτων , Plátōn ; born c. 428–423 BC, died 348/347 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher of Classical Athens who is most commonly considered the foundational thinker of the Western philosophical tradition . [ 1 ] An innovator of the literary dialogue and dialectic forms, Plato influenced all the major areas of theoretical philosophy and practical philosophy , and was the founder of the Academy , a philosophical school in Athens where Plato taught the collection of philosophical theories that would later become known as Platonism .
